clue.text: Friend’s securing check after check – he wins lots, ultimately, in these

indicators.note: To secure something is to hold it fast inside you, so the letters doing the securing close around the ones they hold.
What comes after a thing is written to its right in an across entry, so the piece named first is the one that follows.
Ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter of each word it covers is taken.

blocks.note: CH is how a chess scoresheet marks check, and the clue asks for check twice
the last letters of 'he wins lots' are E, S and S
a friend is a mate, and the ’s hands over the S
the clue's other check, the one the friend secures

explanation.surface: A friend pockets cheque after cheque from a bidder who keeps winning lots at auction.
explanation.walkthrough: Check is CH twice over, once opening the first word and once tucked inside the friend. The definition is a single pointing word, with the picture of somebody racking up wins built around it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'These' is a bare pointer: the contests somebody wins lot after lot in, and a match at the board is exactly such a contest.

clue.text: Singer’s reduced mastery around key

indicators.note: Something reduced has been made smaller, so the word it describes gives up its final letter.
What goes around a thing encircles it, so the letters on the outside close on the one named next.

blocks.note: mastery of a subject is control of it, and reduced it loses its last letter
Alt is one of the keys on a computer keyboard

explanation.surface: A singer whose command of their craft dwindles whenever one particular key comes round.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay are keys on the same keyboard, sitting side by side, which is what makes the join so quiet. 'Key' in a clue about a singer looks musical and is not.
explanation.definitionFit: A contralto is the lowest female voice and also the woman who has it, so the plain word names a person as readily as a range.

clue.text: Optional having European active around English court

indicators.note: To go around something is to enclose it, so the letters named next end up inside rather than alongside.

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for European
a live wire or a live broadcast is an active one
E is the usual abbreviation for English
ct is the shortening of court used in street addresses

explanation.surface: A European player staying busy around an English court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Active' is the word to crack: it reads as a description of the European and is really a synonym waiting to be split open. The court is the ct of a postal address, not the one the surface plays tennis on.
explanation.definitionFit: Something elective is taken by choice rather than required — an elective course, or elective surgery, is the one a person opts into.

clue.text: Light carriage being put out?

blocks.note: read as a vehicle: the little two-wheeled trap raced behind a trotting horse
read as a mood: offended, and letting everybody see it

explanation.surface: A small cart wheeled out of the stable and left standing in the yard.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition arrives in disguise: put out as in offended rather than as in carried outdoors, and the question mark is the setter's nudge towards it. The carriage is the one-seat trap raced behind a trotting horse.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is that racing trap, a frame on two wheels with room for the driver only; the other is the mood of somebody quietly nursing a grievance.

clue.text: Judge Australia to have right measure of information supply

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for Australia on a scoreboard or a car plate
R is the standard abbreviation for right
a bit rate is how fast data arrives, counted in bits per second

explanation.surface: Deciding whether Australia is getting a fair share of broadband capacity.
explanation.walkthrough: The computing term is what hides here, and it arrives whole rather than in pieces: bits per second measure how fast information is supplied. 'Supply' is a noun in that phrase, though the eye wants the adverb from supple.
explanation.definitionFit: To arbitrate is to settle a dispute by deciding between two sides, which is what a judge does, and both words are verbs.

clue.text: Expression of surprise regarding one feature of daffodil

blocks.note: cor is the British exclamation of astonishment, as in 'cor, look at that'
a report on something is a report regarding it
a is the indefinite article, standing in for one

explanation.surface: An astonished noise about one particular part of a daffodil.
explanation.walkthrough: Cor is a British yelp of astonishment worth owning, on call wherever a clue wants three letters of surprise. The part being defined is the frilly trumpet at the centre of the flower, not the petals around it.
explanation.definitionFit: The corona is the botanical name for that trumpet-shaped cup standing proud in the middle of a daffodil.

clue.text: Holderness home to these seabirds?

indicators.note: A place that is home to something has it living inside, so the letters sit within the word rather than beside it.

blocks.note: the letters run unbroken through the middle of the place name

explanation.surface: A stretch of Yorkshire coastline where certain seabirds nest.
explanation.walkthrough: Holderness is the low coastal strip of East Yorkshire running down to Spurn Point, and a place name makes a good hiding place because nobody reads it as letters. The bird itself is the sea eagle.
explanation.definitionFit: An erne is the sea eagle that hunts fish along northern coasts, so a handful of them are seabirds in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Supportive of appropriate gain

blocks.note: somebody pro a policy is supportive of it
a fit punishment is an appropriate one

explanation.surface: Approving of a fair return on the money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' is the one to crack: as an adjective it means fit, though the eye wants the verb, to help yourself to something. The three letters in front are the stock prefix meaning in favour.
explanation.definitionFit: Gain here is the money left when costs come off the takings, the accounting sense of the word rather than any general increase.

clue.text: Prevent hot fighting in midst of battle

indicators.note: In puts one thing within another, so the letters named before it go inside the ones named after.
The midst is the middle, so only the letters at the centre of the word are kept.

blocks.note: the two middle letters of BATTLE are T and T
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
fighting between states is war

explanation.surface: Heated scuffles breaking out in the thick of a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot fighting' looks like one phrase describing the battle and is two separate pieces pointing at two separate chunks. Battle keeps only its centre, which is where the doubled letter comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: To thwart a plan is to stop it going through; the word is only ever used of frustrating somebody else's intention, which is preventing it.

clue.text: Some farmer in search for swill

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it, so a run of letters is taken out of the words rather than all of them.

blocks.note: the letters run straight on through 'farmeR IN SEarch', across two word breaks

explanation.surface: A farmer out looking for pig food.
explanation.walkthrough: Swill is the pig-bucket word on the surface and a verb underneath: to swill a glass out is to rinse it. The hiding place straddles three words, which is where these are hardest to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: To swill something out is to slosh water through it, the same job done to a glass or a bucket, so the two verbs sit on top of each other.

clue.text: Experimental area: year in this removing one’s perplexity

indicators.note: Removing takes something away, so the letters it names come back out of what has just been assembled.

blocks.note: a lab is the room where experiments are done
yr is the standard written short form of year
the two little words are quoted whole, letter for letter
one is I and the ’s is S, and that pair comes off the end

explanation.surface: A year spent in the laboratory curing somebody of their bafflement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In this' is quoted whole, letters and all, which is the step that hides: the phrase is not pointing back at the laboratory. And 'one's' hands over two letters rather than one, the I and the S of the contraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers keeps the figurative sense alongside the maze of windings: any tangle a person cannot think their way out of.

clue.text: Trees beside end of street likely gutted at the outset

indicators.note: The end of a word is its final letter, and that single letter is all this takes.
Something gutted has had its insides pulled out, leaving only the letters at the two edges.

blocks.note: firs are evergreen trees
the final letter of STREET
LIKELY with its insides taken out keeps only the L and the Y

explanation.surface: Trees at the bottom of the street that were probably burnt out early on.
explanation.walkthrough: Three pieces run straight into each other, and the join hides because 'likely' reads as a hedge rather than as a word to be emptied. Firs are the crossword's default trees whenever four letters of woodland are wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the adverb that heads a list, the one used to introduce the first item, which is to say the thing done at the outset.

clue.text: Island I found surrounded by fish in part of Africa

indicators.note: To be found surrounded is to have something on every side, so the letters named next close right around the ones already gathered.

blocks.note: tuna is the fish, and it has to open up to make room
Is. is the abbreviation for island on a map
the letter the clue names outright

explanation.surface: A castaway discovered ringed by fish somewhere off the African coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The fish has to be split to let the other letters in, which is why it acts as the wrapper rather than sitting on one end. Island shortens to a two-letter map abbreviation, not the whole word.
explanation.definitionFit: A country along the North African coast, so the definition is by example: one nation standing in for a piece of the continent.

clue.text: Sadly values-lite, like much broadcasting

indicators.note: Sadly says something has gone wrong, and letters that have gone wrong are letters knocked out of their proper order.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, the hyphen counting for nothing

explanation.surface: A lament that broadcasting these days is short on values.
explanation.walkthrough: The complaint about thin values is itself the fodder, so the words doing the criticising turn into the word for the medium. 'Sadly' does anagram duty while reading as plain regret.
explanation.definitionFit: Televisual means of or suited to television, so it describes what most broadcasting is like: an adjective for the medium itself.

clue.text: Wagner opera is upsetting for one supporter withdrawing name

indicators.note: To upset something is to turn it over, and in a down entry that writes the letters from the bottom up.
Withdrawing is taking back out, so the letter named leaves the word it was sitting in.

blocks.note: the two letters of IS written upwards
eg is the shorthand for 'for example', which is what 'for one' means
a supporter of a cause is a friend of it
N is the abbreviation for name, and it is the letter withdrawn

explanation.surface: A backer so upset by the opera that they take their name off it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' reads as distress and is really an instruction, standing two letters on their head. The opera is the third of Wagner's Ring cycle, named for the hero who kills the dragon.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one named work out of Wagner's catalogue, so the definition is by example: a particular opera standing in for the whole category.

clue.text: Committed pupil pulls back

indicators.note: Back means the other way round, so in an across entry the letters are read from the end to the start.

blocks.note: a tug pulls a barge, so pulls is TOWS, here written in reverse

explanation.surface: A dedicated pupil suddenly hesitating and holding back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulls back' looks like one phrase for hesitating, and the split falls between the words: pulls is the thing to reverse, back the instruction to do it. A swot is British school slang for the pupil who works harder than the others think decent.
explanation.definitionFit: The playground label for the pupil who works far too hard, so it carries the commitment and a sneer about it in the same breath.

clue.text: Beach feature to coil on vacation

blocks.note: to coil a rope is to wind it
somebody on vacation is away on a break

explanation.surface: Something on the beach you roll up once the holiday is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' is the trap: in a cryptic it nearly always means emptied out, and here it means nothing more than on a break. On British beaches the name belongs to the striped canvas screen staked into the sand.
explanation.definitionFit: That screen, hammered into the sand to keep the wind off the picnic, is as much a fixture of a British beach as the deckchair.

clue.text: Image of Jesus church’s taken in two ways – half holy, half mock

indicators.note: Taken in two ways means written forwards and backwards, so the same short piece appears once each way round.

blocks.note: church is CE, and both directions are wanted: EC then CE
the front half of HOLY
the front half of MOCK

explanation.surface: A church's picture of Christ that can be read as devout or as sneering.
explanation.walkthrough: Ecce homo is Pilate's 'behold the man', the Latin tag attached to paintings of Christ crowned with thorns. The two halves that follow are literal halves, the front of each word rather than a synonym for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The words Pilate speaks when presenting the scourged Christ, and so the title art historians give any painting of that moment.

clue.text: This gin gets legions drunk

indicators.note: A drunk cannot hold a straight line, so the letters described that way will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: those seven letters rearranged spell the drink the clue is talking about
the gin is named in the clue, so it comes back out of the seven, and what is left fills the grid

explanation.surface: A gin strong enough to put whole armies on the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines and the whole clue is the wordplay: LEGIONS rearranges into SLOE GIN, so the gin is named and used at once. That shape is called a composite anagram, and the fodder makes the answer plus a word the clue itself supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight it is a true statement: the gin steeped with blackthorn berries, sweet enough that legions really do get drunk on it.

clue.text: Informant about your University is unnaturally sweet

indicators.note: About something means round it, so the letters named first wrap up the ones that follow.

blocks.note: a spy is someone who informs on others
yr is the old letter-writing short form of your
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A tell-tale reporting on your university and being far too nice about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your' shrinking to two letters is the piece to own, an abbreviation out of old correspondence that setters keep in daily use. The informant has to be prised open to take it.
explanation.definitionFit: Syrupy describes sweetness laid on too thick, in a drink or in somebody's manner, which is sweetness pushed past what is natural.

clue.text: Ageing somehow seen linked to knowledge I released

indicators.note: A thing done by no stated route has no stated order either, so the letters may come out in any arrangement.
Released means let go, so the letter it names is let out of the word holding it.

blocks.note: the four letters of SEEN in a new order
science is knowledge, which is exactly what the Latin scientia means
the letter named, released from the middle of that word

explanation.surface: A researcher claiming their published findings explain why we grow old.
explanation.walkthrough: Science standing for knowledge in the literal sense is the step that makes the long chunk findable, and the Latin is the reason it works. The I released is the pronoun taken as a letter, not as a person.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the biologist's word for growing old: the gradual decline of a cell or a body with the years, ageing treated as a process.

clue.text: Repudiate key source of hope we elevated

indicators.note: The source of something is where it starts, so only the opening letter is taken.
Elevated means raised, and raising letters in a down entry writes them from the bottom upwards.

blocks.note: Esc is the escape key at the top left of a keyboard
the first letter of HOPE
the two letters of WE written upwards

explanation.surface: Disowning the very thing the group had raised up as a source of hope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' looks like an adjective propping up 'source of hope' and is a noun, the button top left of the keyboard. Raising 'we' is the last step, since a down entry runs downwards and anything elevated must run against it.
explanation.definitionFit: To eschew something is to keep deliberately clear of it, a settled refusal to have anything to do with it, which is repudiation in practice.

clue.text: One fond of chow initially fond of cartoon dog …

indicators.note: Initially means at the start, and it heads the two words that follow, so each of them gives up nothing but its opening letter.

blocks.note: the initial letters of the two words this instruction stands in front of
Odie is the droopy-eared dog in the Garfield strip

explanation.surface: Someone keen on the chow breed who started out loving a comic-strip dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chow' is the double agent: the surface wants the breed of dog, the definition wants the slang for food. The row of dots hands the cartoon dogs on to the next clue, where another one lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for somebody who takes eating seriously, and chow is slang for the grub itself, so the two words meet on the same register.

clue.text: Rebuke? Republican hitting ceiling

indicators.note: To hit a thing is to come up hard against it, so the piece before is written flush against the piece after.

blocks.note: Rep is the abbreviation beside a Republican's name on an American ballot
the roof of a room is its ceiling seen from the other side

explanation.surface: A Republican losing their temper and going clean through the ceiling.
explanation.walkthrough: Hitting the ceiling is the idiom the surface runs on, and the second chunk is the other word for the same thing, which is why the phrase sounds so natural. The politician shrinks to three letters of ballot paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A reproof is a telling-off delivered to somebody's face, the noun for the words used rather than for the act of saying them.

clue.text: … cartoon dog left in position with repeated character in cartoon

indicators.note: In means inside, so the letter named before it goes within the word named after.
The search runs inside the word cartoon itself, so what is wanted is one of its eight letters rather than a figure drawn in one.

blocks.note: to position something is to put it somewhere
L is the standard abbreviation for left
the one letter that turns up twice in that word

explanation.surface: A cartoon dog kept in place beside a character who keeps coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repeated character in cartoon' means the letter occurring twice in that very word, not a returning member of the cast, and spotting which cartoon is meant is the whole job. The dots tie this back to the clue above, where the other cartoon dog sits.
explanation.definitionFit: Mickey Mouse's dog, drawn by Disney from 1930 onwards, so the definition names the category and the answer supplies one example of it.

clue.text: Old still beer getting mark with pen

blocks.note: ale is beer
M stood for the German mark, the currency Germany used before the euro
Bic is the ballpoint brand, the everyday throwaway pen

explanation.surface: An old flat beer picking up a stain from a biro.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' is the trap: with old and beer on either side it reads as flat and unfizzy, and it is a noun, the vessel. The coin giving the middle letter was retired when the euro came in.
explanation.definitionFit: The bulbous copper vessel alchemists distilled in, so it is a still of the oldest kind rather than any modern apparatus.

clue.text: Upset speaker after cutting off opening

indicators.note: What comes after a cut is what is left once the cut has been made, so the letter named next is gone before the word is read.

blocks.note: a Tannoy is the public-address loudspeaker at a British station or racecourse, the trade name used for any of them
the opening letter of that word, the one cut off

explanation.surface: A speaker put out at having their opening remarks cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speaker' is the person at the lectern on the surface and the loudspeaker underneath: a Tannoy is the trade name that became the ordinary British word for a PA system. 'Upset' is a verb here, which settles what part of speech the answer takes.
explanation.definitionFit: To annoy somebody is to get under their skin, and upset as a verb covers the same low-grade irritation rather than real distress.

clue.text: Thumps one with Guardian heartlessly – it’s a mark of the Greens?

indicators.note: To act heartlessly is to act with the heart taken out, so the inside of the word goes and only its edges are left.

blocks.note: to pound something is to thump it, and the clue's verb keeps its S
I is one in Roman numerals
GUARDIAN with everything between its first and last letters taken out

explanation.surface: Beating somebody about the head with a rolled-up newspaper, quite without mercy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greens' with its capital G wants to be the party, and it is old slang for money, which is what the symbol marks. The paper's name is cut back to its two outer letters, a deeper cut than heartless usually makes.
explanation.definitionFit: £ is the symbol written in front of an amount of sterling, and greens is slang for cash, so what it marks is money rather than a party.

clue.text: Flower from old times getting attention

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
x is the multiplication sign, as in three times four
to keep an eye on something is to keep your attention on it

explanation.surface: Something out of the past that is getting noticed all over again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the trap word: nine times in ten a cryptic means a river, a thing that flows, and here it means the plant. Times as the multiplication cross is the other piece worth owning.
explanation.definitionFit: The big white daisy of British verges and meadows carries this name, so the definition is a plant rather than the usual crossword river.

clue.text: Yes, bad mood may be aggravated by merely adequate historic records

definitions.note: The answer is a single volume, and the plural is fair because the book is nothing but a collection of individual records of who held what.

indicators.note: To aggravate a thing is to make it worse, and letters made worse are letters knocked out of the order they came in.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, taken across the comma
something merely adequate is OK

explanation.surface: A foul temper made worse by something that is only just good enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aggravated' meaning made worse doubles neatly as shaken up, since a mood made worse is a mood disturbed. The record itself is the survey of England that William the Conqueror ordered in 1086, listing who held every field.
explanation.definitionFit: That 1086 survey, village by village and holding by holding, is the oldest public record England has, a whole archive bound up as one volume.
